Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Sri Lanka ordered an end to combat operations against Tamil Tiger rebels in the country's north, the president's office said Monday. But the rebels accused the military of continuing to bomb civilians. Sri Lankan soldiers stand guard next to a tank captured from the Tamil Tigers. "Our security forces have been instructed to end the use of heavy-caliber guns, combat aircraft and aerial weapons which could cause civilian casualties," according a statement from the Presidential Secretariat. A rebel Web site, Tamilnet.com, immediately accused the government of violating its own order and "deceiving the international community." "Two Sri Lanka air force fighter bombers continued to bomb civilian targets in Mu'l'li-vaaykkaal after the announcement by the Sri Lankan forces that it would not deploy heavy weapons or carry out air attacks," Tamilnet said, citing S. Puleedevan, director of the Tamil Peace Secretariat. "Obviously we need to see what that means in practice," John Holmes, the head of U.N. humanitarian operations, said about the government announcement to end combat operations. "But, on the face of it, I think it's good news." The military will now concentrate on "saving" and "rescuing civilians," who have been caught in the fighting between government forces and rebel fighters, the presidential statement said. The government's decision followed an unscheduled meeting of the National Security Council called by President Mahinda Rajapaksa. The session included the commanders of the army, navy and air force. The developments came a day after Sri Lankan officials rejected a proposed cease-fire from the Tamil rebels, warning instead that government troops would continue a new offensive until the group surrendered, a senior government official told CNN. "The government is firm that (the rebels) lay down their arms and surrender. We do not recognize this so-called offer," said Lakshman Hulugalle, director of Sri Lanka's Media Center for National Security. The Tiger leadership had asked the international community to "pressure the Sri Lankan government to reciprocate" on the cease-fire offer. The United States, the United Nations, the European Union and India have called for a cease-fire. The foreign ministers of three nations are due in Sri Lanka on Wednesday -- David Miliband of the United Kingdom, Bernard Kouchner of France and Carl Bildt of Sweden. The rebels' proposed cease-fire came six days after the Sri Lankan army launched a new offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE). Government troops made significant advances into rebel-held territory on Friday and Saturday, according to Sri Lankan army sources. A government-imposed deadline for the Tigers to surrender passed last Tuesday. Tens of thousands of displaced civilians currently remain wedged in a dwindling swath of territory controlled by the Tigers along the country's northeastern coast. Government troops say they have rescued 39,000 civilians trapped in the area, but a U.N. refugee agency said Friday that a wave of "fresh displacement" now exceeds 100,000 people.  Watch civilians describe what they are experiencing » . Fifty metric tons of relief supplies -- which landed in Colombo on Monday -- will be sent by UNICEF to the north to help displaced residents. UNICEF, which called the situation in the north a "catastrophe for children," said the displaced lack food, water and basic medical supplies. The rebels estimate the number of civilians still located in the territory at more than 160,000. The Sri Lankan military said it "freed 3,254 civilians from LTTE clutches" in operations Sunday. The Tigers have been fighting for an independent state in Sri Lanka's northeast since 1983. As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the civil war began, and the group has been declared a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the European Union.

counterfactuals.output:
**Sri Lanka orders halt to heavy combat operations as Tamil Tigers accuse military of continued attacks**

**Colombo, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lanka’s government has ordered an end to the use of heavy weapons, air strikes and combat aircraft in its military campaign against the Tamil Tigers, as international concern grows over the fate of civilians trapped in the shrinking war zone in the country’s northeast.

The government said the decision was intended to protect civilians caught between advancing Sri Lankan troops and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, who have been cornered in a small coastal area after months of intense fighting.

“The security forces have been instructed to end the use of heavy-caliber guns, combat aircraft and aerial weapons that could cause civilian casualties,” the government said in a statement. Officials said operations would continue with the objective of rescuing civilians and defeating the rebels.

But the Tamil Tigers accused the military of continuing attacks on civilian areas despite the announcement. The rebels said shelling and other assaults were still taking place in zones where thousands of civilians remain trapped, allegations the Sri Lankan military has repeatedly denied.

CNN could not independently verify battlefield claims from either side because access to the conflict zone has been severely restricted.

The latest developments come as aid agencies and foreign governments warn of a worsening humanitarian crisis. The United Nations has said large numbers of civilians remain in danger, with limited access to food, clean water and medical care. Hospitals and makeshift treatment centers in the region have reportedly been overwhelmed by the wounded.

Sri Lankan officials accuse the LTTE of using civilians as human shields and preventing them from leaving the conflict area. The rebels deny deliberately endangering civilians and say government attacks are responsible for the mounting casualties.

The LTTE has been fighting for decades to establish an independent homeland for Sri Lanka’s ethnic Tamil minority. The conflict, which began in 1983, has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced many more.

In recent months, the Sri Lankan military has captured nearly all territory once controlled by the rebels, confining the LTTE leadership and remaining fighters to a narrow strip of land along the northeastern coast.

International pressure has intensified on both sides. The United Nations and several governments have called for a pause in fighting to allow civilians to leave safely and permit humanitarian aid to enter the area.

Sri Lanka’s government has rejected calls for a ceasefire, saying any pause would allow the Tigers to regroup. Officials insist the military campaign is close to ending one of Asia’s longest-running civil wars.

For civilians still trapped in the conflict zone, however, the government’s announcement brought little immediate clarity. With accusations continuing and independent monitors absent from the battlefield, the scale of casualties and the true impact of the order remain uncertain.

## Sri Lanka Says It Will Halt Heavy Weapons as War Nears Endgame; Tigers Declare Cease-Fire, UN Urges Civilian Protection

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka — April 2009** — Sri Lanka’s government announced it would stop using heavy weapons, combat aircraft and aerial bombardment in its final offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), as international pressure mounted over the fate of tens of thousands of civilians trapped in the shrinking war zone in the island’s north.

The announcement came during the closing phase of Sri Lanka’s 26-year civil war, with government forces pressing into the LTTE’s last remaining territory along the northeastern coast. The military said it was close to defeating the separatist group, which had fought since the early 1980s for an independent Tamil homeland.

### Government Announces Halt to Heavy Weapons

Sri Lankan authorities said security forces had been instructed to end the use of heavy-caliber guns, combat aircraft and aerial weapons in areas where civilians were present. Officials framed the move as a humanitarian measure designed to protect noncombatants while continuing military operations to rescue civilians and defeat the LTTE.

The government maintained that its operations were aimed at freeing civilians held by the Tigers and insisted that troops would continue advancing using what it described as carefully targeted methods. Colombo rejected calls for a broader cease-fire, arguing that any pause would allow LTTE leaders to regroup or escape.

Sri Lankan officials repeatedly accused the LTTE of using civilians as human shields and preventing them from leaving the conflict zone. The Tigers denied some of those allegations and accused the government of shelling civilian areas.

### LTTE Declares Cease-Fire, Government Dismisses Move

The LTTE announced a unilateral cease-fire, saying it would stop offensive military operations because of the worsening humanitarian situation. The group called on the international community to pressure the Sri Lankan government to halt its assault.

Colombo dismissed the LTTE cease-fire declaration as a “joke” and a tactic by a collapsing organization seeking to avoid defeat. Government leaders said the Tigers had made similar offers in the past when under military pressure and insisted that the LTTE must surrender unconditionally.

The Sri Lankan military continued operations in the remaining conflict zone, where LTTE fighters, senior leaders and large numbers of civilians were believed to be trapped.

### UN Voices Alarm Over Civilian Casualties

The United Nations reacted cautiously to the government’s announcement, welcoming any step that could reduce civilian casualties but urging both sides to ensure the safety of noncombatants. UN officials said the humanitarian situation remained grave, with civilians caught between the advancing army and LTTE positions.

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and senior humanitarian officials called for a pause in fighting to allow civilians to leave safely and to permit aid workers greater access. The UN also pressed the LTTE to allow civilians to depart and urged the Sri Lankan government to respect international humanitarian law.

International agencies warned that food, medicine and clean water were in short supply inside the conflict area. Medical workers reported large numbers of wounded civilians, while access for independent journalists and aid organizations remained severely restricted.

### Massive Civilian Displacement

The final months of the war produced one of the largest displacement crises in Sri Lanka’s history. Tens of thousands of civilians fled the fighting as government troops captured territory formerly controlled by the LTTE. Many crossed into army-held areas exhausted, injured or malnourished.

Those who escaped were sent to government-run camps, including large facilities in the north such as Menik Farm. Sri Lankan authorities described the camps as welfare centers intended to screen civilians for LTTE members and provide shelter, food and medical care.

Human rights groups and foreign governments raised concerns about conditions in the camps, restrictions on movement and the length of time civilians were being held. The government said screening was necessary because LTTE combatants could be hiding among civilians.

At the height of the crisis, estimates of civilians trapped in the war zone varied widely. The government gave lower figures, while the United Nations and humanitarian organizations suggested that far larger numbers remained at risk.

### International Pressure Intensifies

The United States, Britain, France, India, the European Union and the United Nations all increased diplomatic pressure on Sri Lanka as the offensive neared its conclusion. Foreign governments urged Colombo to protect civilians, allow humanitarian access and consider a temporary pause in fighting.

Britain and France pushed for stronger international action and called for a humanitarian cease-fire. India, with its large Tamil population in the southern state of Tamil Nadu, also pressed Sri Lanka to minimize civilian casualties while balancing its strategic relationship with Colombo.

Sri Lanka resisted outside pressure, saying the war was an internal matter and that the government was on the verge of eliminating a group widely designated as terrorist by several countries. Officials argued that international calls for a cease-fire risked prolonging the conflict.

China, Pakistan and some other states continued to support Sri Lanka diplomatically and, in some cases, militarily, helping Colombo withstand Western pressure at international forums.

### War Nears Its Conclusion

By late April and May 2009, the LTTE had been reduced to a narrow strip of coastal territory in Mullaitivu district. The group’s conventional military capacity had largely collapsed after a series of battlefield defeats, including the loss of Kilinochchi, its de facto administrative capital, earlier in the year.

Sri Lankan forces eventually captured the remaining territory in May 2009. The government announced that LTTE leader Velupillai Prabhakaran had been killed and declared the war over.

The final offensive ended the LTTE as a conventional fighting force but left deep controversy over civilian casualties, alleged violations of international humanitarian law, the treatment of displaced Tamils and the prospects for political reconciliation. Years later, the final months of the war remained the subject of international scrutiny, competing casualty claims and calls for accountability from human rights organizations and UN bodies.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

## Sri Lankan Offensive Traps Civilians as Government Pushes Against Tamil Tigers

**Colombo, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lankan government forces pressed deeper into the island’s north as they sought to crush the remaining strongholds of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, while international officials warned that tens of thousands of civilians were trapped in the shrinking battle zone.

The military said its troops were advancing on rebel-held territory in the northeast after months of fighting that has brought the government closer than ever to defeating the separatist movement, which has waged a decades-long war for an independent Tamil homeland.

Sri Lankan officials said the offensive was aimed at ending terrorism and freeing civilians being held by the rebels. The LTTE, however, accused the government of shelling civilian areas and creating a humanitarian catastrophe.

Independent verification of battlefield claims remained difficult because journalists and most aid agencies have been barred from the conflict zone.

### Civilians caught in shrinking territory

The United Nations and humanitarian organizations have expressed growing alarm over the fate of civilians trapped between advancing government troops and LTTE fighters.

U.N. officials have said civilians are facing severe shortages of food, water and medicine, with makeshift hospitals overwhelmed by casualties. Aid workers have warned that many families have been displaced multiple times and are sheltering in bunkers or open areas with little protection from artillery fire.

A U.N. spokesperson urged both sides to protect civilians and allow humanitarian access, saying civilians must be permitted to leave the fighting area safely and voluntarily.

Foreign governments have also called for restraint. Officials from the United States, Britain, India and the European Union have urged Sri Lanka to avoid civilian casualties and pressed the LTTE to allow noncombatants to move out of areas under its control.

### Government: Rebels using civilians as shields

Sri Lankan government officials rejected accusations that the military was deliberately targeting civilians. They said troops were carrying out a carefully planned operation against a banned terrorist group and accused the LTTE of using civilians as human shields.

“The responsibility for the suffering of civilians lies with the terrorists who are preventing them from leaving,” a government official said, according to state media. Officials said safe passages had been opened for civilians and that thousands had crossed into government-controlled areas.

The government has described the campaign as the final phase of its war against the LTTE, which once controlled large areas of northern and eastern Sri Lanka and operated a conventional fighting force, naval wing and suicide squads.

Sri Lankan authorities say the rebels have been weakened by battlefield losses, defections and the loss of key supply routes.

### LTTE: Government attacks civilian zones

The LTTE denied holding civilians by force and accused the military of indiscriminate bombardment. Rebel representatives appealed for international intervention and called for a ceasefire, saying the civilian population in the north was under siege.

The group said hospitals and densely populated areas had been hit in government attacks. Sri Lankan officials have repeatedly denied targeting hospitals or civilians and say the rebels have fired from civilian areas.

The LTTE, which has been designated a terrorist organization by several countries, including the United States and members of the European Union, has been blamed for suicide bombings, political assassinations and attacks on civilians during the conflict.

### Calls for ceasefire grow

As the fighting intensified, international pressure mounted on both sides.

U.N. officials called for humanitarian pauses in the fighting to evacuate the wounded and deliver aid. Foreign diplomats urged the Sri Lankan government to allow greater access for international monitors and relief agencies.

Human rights groups accused both the government and the LTTE of violating the laws of war. They said the rebels must stop preventing civilians from leaving and that the government must halt the use of heavy weapons in areas where civilians are concentrated.

Sri Lankan officials have resisted calls for a ceasefire, arguing that any pause would allow the LTTE to regroup. The government has said military operations will continue until the rebels surrender or are defeated.

### War nearing decisive stage

The conflict between the Sri Lankan state and the LTTE has lasted more than a quarter-century, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing hundreds of thousands more.

The LTTE said it was fighting discrimination against the Tamil minority by the Sinhalese-dominated state. Successive Sri Lankan governments accused the group of pursuing separatism through terrorism and refusing political compromise.

With the rebels now confined to a small area in the north, the government has portrayed victory as imminent. But aid agencies say the cost to civilians could be devastating unless both sides take urgent steps to protect them.

For families trapped in the war zone, the immediate concern is survival: finding shelter from shelling, caring for the wounded and searching for a route to safety.

As one humanitarian official put it, “The military battle may be nearing its end, but the civilian crisis is far from over.”

Sri Lanka’s government has instructed its armed forces to stop using heavy-caliber guns, combat aircraft, and aerial weapons in operations against the Tamil Tiger rebels, officials said, as concerns mounted over civilian casualties in the country’s northern war zone.

President Mahinda Rajapaksa’s administration said the order was intended to protect civilians trapped in the shrinking area still held by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE. The rebels, who have fought for decades to create an independent Tamil state, have been cornered by a major military offensive.

The government said security forces would continue operations aimed at defeating the LTTE but would rely on methods intended to minimize harm to noncombatants. International organizations and foreign governments had repeatedly urged both sides to allow civilians to leave the conflict zone and to avoid indiscriminate attacks.

The LTTE has been accused of using civilians as human shields, while the Sri Lankan military has faced allegations that shelling and airstrikes caused heavy civilian casualties. Both sides have denied or disputed various accusations during the final stages of the war.

The announcement came as Sri Lankan forces pressed deeper into rebel-held territory, with the government claiming it was close to ending the decades-long conflict. Humanitarian agencies warned that thousands of civilians remained at risk, with limited access to food, medical care, and safe passage out of the fighting.

**Sri Lanka Rejects Tamil Tiger Cease-Fire Offer, Presses Offensive in Northeast**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka, Jan. 27 —** Sri Lanka’s government rejected a cease-fire offer from the Tamil Tiger rebels and vowed to continue its military offensive in the island’s northeast, where troops were pushing deeper into the separatists’ shrinking enclave and officials said hundreds of civilians had escaped the fighting.

The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, had called for a cease-fire amid growing international concern over civilians trapped in the battle zone. But the government dismissed the offer as an attempt by the rebels to regroup after a series of battlefield defeats.

Defense officials said the military would accept nothing short of the Tigers laying down their weapons and releasing civilians under their control.

“The LTTE must surrender,” government officials said, describing the cease-fire proposal as a tactic intended to halt advancing troops rather than a genuine move toward peace.

The rejection came as Sri Lankan forces continued operations in the northern district of Mullaittivu, the last major area still contested by the rebels after the military captured a succession of LTTE strongholds, including Kilinochchi, the Tigers’ former administrative capital, earlier in the campaign.

The army said troops were advancing on remaining rebel positions and had opened routes for civilians to flee the combat zone. Military spokesmen said hundreds of people had crossed into government-held territory in recent days, many of them exhausted and in need of food, shelter and medical care.

The government accused the LTTE of holding civilians as human shields, an allegation the rebels have repeatedly denied. Aid agencies have warned that tens of thousands of civilians may be trapped in a rapidly shrinking area with limited access to food, clean water and medical assistance.

The United Nations Children’s Fund said it was delivering emergency supplies for displaced families and children affected by the fighting. UNICEF and other humanitarian agencies have been attempting to move aid into government-controlled areas and assist civilians who have fled the front lines, though access to the conflict zone itself has been heavily restricted.

UNICEF officials said relief deliveries included essential supplies such as hygiene materials, nutritional support and other assistance for displaced families, with children considered especially vulnerable because of displacement, malnutrition and exposure to violence.

International pressure has grown on both sides to protect civilians. The United Nations, foreign governments and human rights groups have called for safe passage for noncombatants and urged the combatants to comply with humanitarian law.

Sri Lanka’s government says the offensive is close to ending one of Asia’s longest-running insurgencies. The LTTE has fought since the early 1980s for an independent homeland for the island’s ethnic Tamil minority, saying Tamils faced discrimination and abuses by successive Sinhalese-dominated governments.

The conflict erupted into full-scale civil war in 1983 and has killed tens of thousands of people. The Tigers at one point controlled large areas of northern and eastern Sri Lanka and operated a de facto state with its own police, courts and taxation system. The group also developed a naval wing and a small air capability, making it one of the most organized insurgent movements in the world.

But the LTTE has been widely condemned for suicide bombings, assassinations, child recruitment and attacks on civilians. It is banned as a terrorist organization by several countries, including the United States, India and members of the European Union. The Tigers were blamed for the 1991 assassination of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and the 1993 killing of Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa.

A Norwegian-brokered cease-fire signed in 2002 raised hopes for a negotiated settlement, but the truce gradually collapsed amid mutual accusations of violations, political killings and renewed fighting. Sri Lanka formally withdrew from the agreement in 2008, and the military intensified its campaign to dismantle LTTE-controlled territory.

Government forces have since made rapid gains, seizing rebel supply routes, coastal positions and command centers. Officials in Colombo say the Tigers are now cornered in a small area of jungle and coastline in the northeast.

The rebels, however, have said they continue to resist and have accused the government of causing civilian casualties through shelling and aerial attacks. Sri Lankan authorities deny deliberately targeting civilians and say troops are conducting a “humanitarian operation” to free civilians from LTTE control.

Independent verification of claims from either side remains difficult because journalists and most aid workers have limited access to the front lines.

As the offensive continues, humanitarian agencies say the immediate priority is civilian protection. Aid officials have warned that displaced families arriving in government areas require urgent support, while those still trapped inside the conflict zone face worsening conditions as fighting intensifies.
